passage:
Dear Yamini di,
You said to write when college got hard, so here it is. Last week I got a fever in the hostel. My roommate had gone home, and I lay alone in the dark, sweating and shivering, feeling about seven years old. I wanted Amma's rasam so badly I cried. I didn't tell anyone. I kept thinking: everyone's busy, I'm an adult, don't make a fuss. By the second night I couldn't get up to fill my bottle. That scared me. I finally messaged my friend Arvind down the corridor. He came with water and told the warden, and she took me to the campus clinic that morning. I'm better now. Next time I won't wait. I'll message someone straight away.
Love,
Sumit

qa.q: Who did Sumit finally message?
qa.a: Arvind, a friend down the corridor.

qa.q: Why didn't Sumit tell anyone at first?
qa.a: Sumit felt lonely and homesick but reluctant to bother anyone, thinking everyone was busy and an adult should not make a fuss.

qa.q: What will Sumit do differently, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Message someone straight away next time, because reaching out early makes being ill safer and less lonely.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel reading this?
qa.a: She would probably feel worried for Sumit but relieved that Arvind and the warden helped, and glad Sumit wrote.

grounding: Shows a student sick alone in a hostel feeling homesick and reluctant to bother anyone, and learning that reaching out early is safer.

passage: Sudha, it's Kunal. You're moving into the hostel next week, so let me tell you about my first fever there. Second month, I woke up burning, every bone aching. My roommate was away. I lay there scrolling photos of Mumma's kitchen, so homesick it hurt more than the fever, and feeling very sorry for myself. I didn't text anyone. I thought they'd call me a baby. By evening I was dizzy walking to the bathroom. Then the warden, Mr D'Souza, knocked, because I'd missed dinner and he'd noticed. He took one look, called the doctor on duty and made me phone home. Mumma cried, then made me promise something. So here's the promise I'm passing on: if you're ill, tell your roommate, the warden or home that same day. Nobody will think you're a baby.

qa.q: Why did the warden knock?
qa.a: Kunal had missed dinner, and the warden noticed.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling alone in the room?
qa.a: Kunal felt deeply homesick and full of self-pity, and afraid of seeming like a baby.

qa.q: What advice does Kunal pass on, and why is it sound?
qa.a: To tell a roommate, the warden or home the same day when ill, because reaching out early makes recovery safer and less lonely.

qa.q: How did Mr D'Souza's noticing change things?
qa.a: He noticed the missed dinner, called the doctor on duty and got Kunal to phone home, turning a lonely night into getting help.

grounding: Illustrates a student ill alone in a hostel feeling homesick, full of self-pity and reluctant to bother anyone, and the case for reaching out early.

passage:
Dear Vidya Api,
I'm writing this from my hostel bed with a cup of the warden's ginger tea, so don't panic: I'm getting better.
On Tuesday I woke up with a fever and a sore throat and decided not to tell anyone. You're busy with the baby, Ammi would worry, and my roommate is away. By evening I was lying in the dark crying over a video of Ammi's biryani, missing home so much it hurt, and feeling sorry for myself in a very dramatic way.
Then I remembered you saying, "Tell someone early, not late." So I called the warden. She came within ten minutes, took me to the campus clinic, and has checked on me twice a day since. My friend Tejal brings soup.
I still miss home. But I don't feel alone anymore.
Love,
Zeenat

qa.q: Who brings Zeenat soup?
qa.a: Zeenat's friend Tejal.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling on Tuesday evening?
qa.a: Zeenat felt homesick and full of self-pity, crying in the dark over a video of Ammi's biryani.

qa.q: What turned things around for Zeenat?
qa.a: Remembering to tell someone early and calling the warden, who took Zeenat to the campus clinic and kept checking in.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Vidya may feel a pang of worry, then relief and pride that Zeenat asked for help.

grounding: Shows a student sick alone in a hostel feeling homesick and reluctant to bother anyone, then reaching out to the warden and a friend.

passage: You want to know the worst week of first year? Easy. I'm Ganga, the girl from Kannur who thought she was too grown-up to be homesick. Then in November I got a stomach bug in the hostel. Everyone had gone home for the long weekend. I lay there shivering, too weak to walk to the mess, texting my mother "all fine" because I didn't want her crying on the phone. By the second night I was talking to the ceiling fan and crying about my grandmother's rice gruel. I felt so stupid. Finally I texted Tejas, just "are you on campus?" He came in fifteen minutes with water bottles and bananas, then marched me to the warden, who called the doctor. The lesson? Tell people on day one, not day two. Being sick alone is miserable. Being sick and pretending is worse.

qa.q: What did Tejas bring?
qa.a: Water bottles and bananas.

qa.q: Why did Ganga text "all fine" to her mother?
qa.a: Ganga didn't want to worry her mother and felt too grown-up to be homesick, even while feeling miserable and lonely.

qa.q: What is Ganga's lesson, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Tell people on day one, not day two, because reaching out early makes being sick safer and less lonely.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt getting the text "are you on campus?"
qa.a: Tejas probably sensed something was wrong and felt worried, coming within fifteen minutes.

grounding: Shows a student sick alone in a hostel, homesick and reluctant to bother anyone, and learning to reach out early.

passage:
Sunday: Alka woke in her Pune hostel with a fever and a pounding head. Her roommate had gone home. She told herself it was nothing and didn't want to bother anyone. She lay under two blankets scrolling through old photos of her mother's garden in Shillong, crying quietly.
Monday: Worse. She skipped classes. When Francis texted, "missing u in lab, all ok?", she typed "yes" and then deleted it. She typed "actually no, I'm sick" and sent that.
Tuesday: Francis had told the warden on Monday evening, and the warden had taken Alka to the doctor that night. Now Francis sat by her bed copying lab notes while Alka sipped soup and video-called her mother. She still missed home. But the room felt less empty.

qa.q: What did Francis text on Monday?
qa.a: "missing u in lab, all ok?"

qa.q: What was Alka feeling on Sunday?
qa.a: She felt homesick and lonely, crying quietly over photos of her mother's garden, and reluctant to bother anyone.

qa.q: What was the turning point?
qa.a: Deleting "yes" and telling Francis the truth, which led to the warden and a doctor's visit that night.

qa.q: How might Francis feel sitting by Alka's bed?
qa.a: Francis is probably relieved to have been trusted and glad to keep Alka company.

grounding: Shows a student sick alone in a hostel, homesick and unwilling to bother anyone, whose honest reply to a friend brings help.

passage: Ojas, before you leave for your hostel, let your Sarika Bua tell you one thing. In my second year at college in Pune, I caught a fever in the monsoon. I lay in my room for two days, shivering, eating dry biscuits, crying for my mother's rasam. I didn't tell anyone. Why bother the warden, I thought, why worry Amma two hundred kilometres away? On the third morning my roommate Kavita found me too weak to stand. She fetched the warden, who took me to the doctor that same hour and phoned Amma. Amma came on the evening bus. I felt foolish for waiting. So promise me: if you're sick, you tell a friend, the warden or us on the very first day.

qa.q: What did young Sarika eat while ill?
qa.a: Dry biscuits.

qa.q: Why didn't young Sarika tell anyone she was sick?
qa.a: She felt reluctant to bother the warden or worry Amma, even while homesick and crying for her mother's rasam.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sarika's hostel story?
qa.a: Kavita finding her and fetching the warden, who took her to the doctor and phoned Amma the same hour.

qa.q: How might Kavita have felt finding Sarika too weak to stand?
qa.a: Kavita was probably alarmed and worried, which is why she fetched the warden at once.

grounding: An aunt recalls being sick alone in a hostel, homesick and reluctant to bother anyone, and urges reaching out early.
